edges.relationship: Relates the baby boom to child-centred households, consumer markets and psychological ideas about childhood.
edges.evidence_note: Daniel Stoffman describes these arguments in his substantive review; this is named-reader mediation, not a reading of the whole book. He questions how distinctive the cohort itself was.

edges.relationship: Interprets Canadian youth politics through the scale and shared culture of the baby-boom generation.
edges.evidence_note: Stoffman reports the interpretation but disputes the space given to radicals and the claim of broad generational sympathy. The qualification is part of this contribution record.

edges.relationship: Examines everyday gatekeeping and the contested remaking of immigrant citizenship in Cold War Canada.
edges.evidence_note: Basok and Bastable’s substantive reading of Gatekeepers supports this scoped claim, including immigrant negotiation/resistance; it is not full-book verification.

edges.relationship: Places gendered expectations about marriage, family and sexuality inside the regulation of newcomers.
edges.evidence_note: The same review’s treatment of Gatekeepers makes these mechanisms substantive, rather than inferring a gender arrow from Iacovetta’s appointment.

edges.relationship: Studies African labour and exploitation without assuming universal proletarianization.
edges.evidence_note: Cooper’s opening autobiographical answers distinguish post-slavery labour, land and uneven colonial power.

edges.relationship: Treats empire and citizenship relationally across scales and alternative political possibilities.
edges.evidence_note: The interview’s citizenship and historical-sequences answers warn against reading national outcomes backwards. Coauthored books retain Jane Burbank’s credit.

edges.relationship: Interprets Reconstruction through Black political action, contested freedom and the struggle to build democracy.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview answers stress change after slavery and oppose treating later injustice as proof that emancipation changed nothing.

edges.relationship: Traces competing meanings of freedom rather than treating freedom as one stable national possession.
edges.evidence_note: In the interview Foner explicitly contrasts economic equality and rights with narrow anti-government definitions, and rejects narratives that absorb every struggle into a stable Americanism.

edges.relationship: Tracks the late-twentieth-century fragmentation of ideas about markets, society, identities and historical constraint.
edges.evidence_note: Author’s 2011 account specifies intellectual arguments and changing categories; not simply a party-political change.

edges.relationship: Links shifting concepts of obligation and choice to arguments over social provision and public policy.
edges.evidence_note: Rorotoko statement expressly connects fracturing thought to school choice, safety nets, affirmative action and war; policy examples are his interpretations.

edges.relationship: Distinguishes gender history’s analysis of produced sexual difference from recovery of women’s participation alone.
edges.evidence_note: Own university interview explicitly makes the methodological distinction.

edges.relationship: Connects historical gender categories and divisions of labour to slavery and imperial power.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview explains this specific connection; no blanket claim that every empire shared an identical gender regime.

edges.relationship: Critically reworks the economic-conflict interpretation and explores ideological consensus in American politics.
edges.evidence_note: Foner distinguishes Hofstadter’s critical consensus interpretation from celebratory versions and notes the later reconsideration of conflict.

edges.relationship: Brings status anxiety, symbols and irrationality into accounts of political culture.
edges.evidence_note: Foner’s named substantive reading also judges the treatment of Populists and Progressives exaggerated and elitist in important respects. This qualification survives the contribution arrow.

edges.relationship: Relates emancipation and the eight-hour movement to broader struggles over labour freedom.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview credits Du Bois’s general-strike interpretation; no claim that emancipation mechanically caused every later labour development.

edges.relationship: Examines white-worker identity as historically constructed and as a constraint on class solidarity.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview distinguishes historical racialization from natural race and explicitly denies race explains everything about labour conservatism.

edges.relationship: Makes changing sensory experience—smells, bells and desires—a historical question.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview expressly declines exclusive priority and situates the questions in wider historiographical circumstances.

edges.relationship: Experiments with recovering the world of a person who left no self-authored archive.
edges.evidence_note: Own account of Pinagot explains the wish to recover an unknown individual; reconstructed context is not that person’s recorded inner voice.

edges.relationship: Questions histories that make recovering agency the endpoint of interpreting slavery.
edges.evidence_note: Read article, especially opening problem and closing methodological discussion; criticism is of an analytic habit rather than of enslaved action itself.

edges.relationship: Calls for historically specific accounts of enslaved humanity, action and collective life beyond the agency/resistance formula.
edges.evidence_note: Read article’s distinction between humanity and agency, with its caution about liberal notions of autonomous selfhood. This is a methodological contribution to slavery history, not a claim every case has been independently verified.
